newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Child labour conference ends on a hopeful note.
newsitem.headline: Child labour conference ends on a hopeful note.

text.p: An international conference on child labour ended on Thursday with delegates expressing guarded optimism that the worst forms of exploiting 250 million working children worldwide can be stopped.

"Because the causes of child labour are complex, including poverty, social values and even cultural complacency, there can be no simple or single answers," Carol Bellamy, executive director of the U.N. Children's Fund (Unicef) said.

"But two things are obvious -- first, that the exploitation of children in hazardous work is totally unacceptable, and second, that it can be stopped," she told the final session of the two-day conference in Amsterdam.
"Hazardous child labour is a betrayal of every child's rights as a human being and is an offence against our civilization," she added.
The conference has focused on the most intolerable types of child labour -- slavery, forced labour and the use of children in prostitution, pornography and drug trafficking.

It called for an immediate end to such practices and hoped that discussions started between the 200 government ministers, union leaders and childrens' representatives present would help lay the groundwork for a worldwide ban.
Delegates have said this could now happen because of a sea-change in attitudes to the problem.
"Those of us who remember what the situation was like a decade ago, remember a few individual voices crying in the wilderness," said Assefa Bequele of the International Labour Office (ILO).
"But now the issue has jumped to the top of the international agenda. I think it can be stated that the battle against child labour is being won."
International action has long been complicated by fears among developing countries that it may be used to undermine their main advantage in world trade -- cheap labour.

India's Labour Minister M. Arunachalam told the conference: "Parents send children away to work instead of sending them to school not because they want it, but because there is no option or alternative for their biological survival."
But improving access to education was one of the keys to solving the problem of child labour, Bellamy said.
Unicef says 30 percent of children in developing countries who enrol in primary school do not complete it and over 100 million children -- 60 percent of them girls --- do not attend school at all.
Bequele warned that the ILO estimate of 250 million children between five and 14 at work was probably well below the actual figure.

A background report prepared for the conference says tens of millions of child labourers are still kept as slaves or under forced labour systems such as debt bondage, where children work to pay off a family obligation.
The commercial sexual exploitation of children was also increasing, with organised networks trading in children both nationally and internationally.

"To call these practices 'child labour' is far too mild," German Labour Minister Norbert Blum told the conference. "Debt bondage is slavery. Child prostitution can be murder. You can kill a person's mind and soul as surely as their body."
A follow-up conference will be held in Oslo in October at which it is hoped to draft an international commitment to eradicate all child work.
But some delegates said international initiatives would achieve little without more concerted efforts at local level.
"Nearly every country has ratified the (U.N.) Convention on the Rights of the Child," Bellamy said.
"If governments would even deliver on the commitments they have already made...we could be looking at a world free of child labour in the next few years."
